name: Traffic Grid
miniText: The scientific question is whether signal timing and vehicle density jointly determine urban-grid congestion. In NetLogo's Traffic Grid model, cars accelerate and follow other vehicles while stopping at red lights, whose phases can be controlled locally or automatically. The selected literature connects this mechanism to network congestion and signal coordination: grid interactions can generate a transition to collective blockage [1]; self-organizing traffic lights provide a contrasting control strategy [2]; microscopic traffic-state comparisons caution against uncalibrated travel predictions [3]. Regular roads, simplified car following and limited route choice omit heterogeneous trips and intersections; waiting counts and throughput measure different objectives. The original NetLogo behavior is the baseline for reimplementation. This simulation offers a controlled thought experiment, and agreement with its output does not establish empirical validation.

verification.evidenceSummary: Steering traffic in cities is a very complex task, since improving efficiency involves the coordination of many actors. Traditional approaches attempt to optimize traffic lights for a particular density and configuration of traffic. The disadvantage of this lies in the fact that traffic densities and configurations change constantly. Traffic seems to be an adaptation problem rather than an optimization problem. We propose a simple and feasible alternative, in which traffic lights self-organize to improve traffic flow. We use a multi-agent simulation to study three self-organizing methods, which are able to outperform traditional rigid and adaptive methods. Using simple rules and no direct communication, traffic lights are able to self-organize and adapt to changing traffic conditions, reducing waiting times, number of stopped cars, and increasing average speeds.
